rewrite.misconception: Changing an environment variable remains a safe standard library call in edition 2024.

cards.statement: For a local `p` whose struct type lacks a `Drop` impl, `let x = p.a;` leaves the `String` field `p.b` usable.
cards.explanation: For a struct without Drop held in a local variable, Rust tracks each field separately, so moving out one field leaves the others usable, though not the whole struct.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. Checked on Reference field-expr: 'If the struct does not implement Drop and is stored in a local variable, this also applies to moving out of each of its fields.' Both conditions are in the statement, and the answer is True whether p.a is moved or copied.

cards.statement: `let a = &mut s; let b = &mut s;` compiles when `a` is still used after `b` is created.
cards.explanation: The first mutable borrow of s stays live until a's last use, so creating b in the meantime is a second simultaneous &mut borrow, which the borrow checker rejects.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. The statement matches the Book ch04-02 r1/r2 example, where the first mutable borrow lasts until its later use and the second &mut s is rejected. The reborrow loophole is closed.

cards.statement: In `fn head(s: &str, n: usize) -> &str`, elision ties the returned reference to the lifetime of `s`.
cards.explanation: Only one lifetime appears among the parameters, since usize holds none, so elision assigns it to the elided output and the signature needs no annotation.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. The Reference lifetime-elision page states the exactly-one-lifetime rule and gives substr1(s: &str, until: usize) -> &str expanding to &'a str, which is the same shape. Input and output are both elided, so mismatched_lifetime_syntaxes does not fire.

cards.statement: For an array with enough elements, `&a[1..=3]` includes the element at index 3.
cards.explanation: The start..=end syntax builds a RangeInclusive, which contains its end value, so slicing with 1..=3 borrows the elements at indexes 1, 2 and 3.
cards.reason: Both lenses flag the source: the Reference range-expr page has no slicing example. I moved the source to 'RangeInclusive in std::ops - Rust' (https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/ops/struct.RangeInclusive.html). I fetched it and it says 'start..=end contains all values with x >= start and x <= end' and shows assert_eq!(arr[1..=3], [1, 2, 3]). I used the fact lens's explanation because it can be checked against that page. The statement and answer are unchanged.

cards.statement: A second inherent `impl` block can replace a struct's previously defined methods.
cards.explanation: Inherent impl blocks for one type add their items together. Reusing a method name that an earlier impl block of the type already defines is a duplicate definition the compiler rejects.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. I fetched E0592: two impl Foo blocks both defining bar give 'duplicate definition here'. The page is official and on doc.rust-lang.org but outside the six listed doc sets. Neither lens asks to drop for that, and the Reference only says multiple inherent impls are allowed. The explanation names no error code.

cards.statement: Inside `fn run<F: FnOnce()>(f: F)`, passing `f` to a parameter bounded by `Fn()` compiles.
cards.explanation: Fn has FnMut and FnOnce as supertraits, so every Fn type also satisfies FnOnce. A type known only to be FnOnce gives no Fn guarantee, so the call is rejected.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. The std Fn page has 'pub trait Fn<Args>: FnMut<Args>' and names FnMut and FnOnce as supertraits of Fn. The implication goes only one way, so an F bounded only by FnOnce fails an Fn() bound. The statement now asks about one direction only.

cards.statement: When code assigns a new `String` to `s`, Rust frees the old buffer at the end of `s`'s scope.
cards.explanation: Replacing an existing String drops its previous value immediately. Its old allocation is released during the assignment.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. Book ch04-01: assigning a completely new value to an existing variable makes Rust call drop and free the original value's memory immediately. The tell word is removed and the fact is unchanged.

cards.statement: `#[derive(Default)]` on an enum makes its first unit variant the default value.
cards.explanation: Derived Default needs a #[default] marker on a unit variant; declaration order does not select the value. Default::default() returns the marked variant.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. The std Default docs say that with #[derive(Default)] on an enum you choose the default unit variant by placing #[default] on it. The 'automatically' template is gone and the fact is unchanged.

cards.statement: Marking a struct `pub` makes its fields part of the struct's public API.
cards.explanation: pub makes the struct type public while its fields retain their own visibility. Mark a field pub to expose that field through the public API.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. Book ch07-03: 'If we use pub before a struct definition, we make the struct public, but the struct's fields will still be private.' The 'automatically' template is gone and the fact is unchanged.

cards.statement: In the 2024 edition, the prelude brings `Future` and `IntoFuture` into scope.
cards.explanation: Rust 2024's standard prelude includes Future and IntoFuture. The compiler makes those traits available through the prelude in ordinary module code.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. The Edition Guide page rust-2024/prelude lists std::future::Future and std::future::IntoFuture as added to the 2024 prelude. Only a redundant 'automatically' was removed.
